nameStory: The "sickle-tailed" millipede gets its dramatic name from the curved, blade-like appendages at the rear end of males, which resemble tiny farming sickles. These specialized structures are used during mating and give this otherwise humble soil-dweller a surprisingly fierce-sounding name. The species name "canadensis" hints at its northern origins, though it ventures south into New England's cooler forests.
description: The sickle-tailed millipede is a slender, worm-like creature that coils into a tight spiral when disturbed. Growing about 1-2 inches long, it has a smooth, shiny reddish-brown to dark brown body divided into many segments, each bearing two pairs of tiny legs. Unlike centipedes, millipedes are gentle decomposers that slowly crawl through leaf litter and soil, helping break down dead plant material. You'll recognize it as a millipede by its rounded body and slow, wave-like movement.

idTips.label: Sickle-shaped tail structures
idTips.description: Males have distinctive curved, pointed projections at the rear that feel firm and horn-like when gently touched - these are the "sickles" that give the species its name

idTips.label: Coiling behavior
idTips.description: When threatened, rolls into a tight, flat spiral like a watch spring - you can gently uncoil it and it will slowly curl back up

idTips.label: Body texture and color
idTips.description: Smooth, glossy surface that feels slightly waxy to the touch, ranging from reddish-brown to dark chocolate brown with a subtle sheen

idTips.label: Size and proportions
idTips.description: Slender build, about as thick as a pencil lead, reaching 1-2 inches when fully extended - noticeably thinner than most other millipedes

idTips.label: Movement pattern
idTips.description: Moves in slow, rhythmic waves with legs moving in coordinated ripples from front to back - much slower than a centipede's darting motion

habitat: Look for sickle-tailed millipedes in cool, moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly under rotting logs, leaf litter, and loose bark. They prefer areas with rich, dark soil and plenty of decomposing organic matter, often found alongside other small soil creatures in the top few inches of forest floor. They're most common in northern New England's higher elevation forests but can be found in suitable microhabitats throughout the region.

seasonality.spring: Active as soil warms, often found under logs and stones where they've overwintered. Look for them during mild, damp days when they venture closer to the surface.
seasonality.summer: Most active period, especially after rain when they may be found crawling on the surface of trails or under freshly fallen logs. Peak time for observing the distinctive sickle structures on mature males.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move deeper into soil and under more substantial cover as they prepare for winter. Good time to find them in thick leaf litter.
seasonality.winter: Dormant and hidden deep in soil or under large logs and stones. Rarely seen unless you dig into protected areas on warmer winter days.

funFact: Despite having hundreds of legs, millipedes like this one are actually terrible at walking in a straight line - they naturally spiral as they move because their legs on one side are slightly shorter than the other, causing them to walk in gentle curves even when trying to go forward!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small millipedes, but the sickle-shaped tail projections on males are unique. Remember: if it coils up, moves slowly, and has the distinctive "sickles," you've found your species - centipedes run fast and don't coil into flat spirals.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents one of the least-studied millipede groups in New England, with only a single documented observation in our region. Many millipede species are still being discovered and described by scientists, so finding one could contribute valuable information about New England's hidden biodiversity.
compareHints: As the only Uroblaniulus species documented in New England, compare it with other small parajulid millipedes by looking for the distinctive sickle-shaped tail structures. Most other regional millipedes in this family lack such prominent rear projections and tend to be either much larger or have different body proportions. The combination of slender build, glossy surface, and those telltale "sickles" makes this species unique among New England's millipede fauna.
